html:
The Emirate of Córdoba was the Muslim state that ruled most of the Iberian Peninsula from 756 to 929, under a branch of the Umayyad family. On the map for 800 and 900 it covers most of Spain and Portugal.

When the Abbasids overthrew the Umayyad Caliphate in 750 and killed most of its family, a young prince, Abd al-Rahman, escaped to al-Andalus and took power in 756. He refused to obey Baghdad and began the Great Mosque of Córdoba.

His successors built Córdoba into one of the largest cities of Europe, with new crops, irrigation and trade. They faced revolts by local converts and Arab and Berber factions, raids by the Vikings, who sacked Seville in 844, and the Christian kingdom of Asturias in the north. In 929 Abd al-Rahman III declared himself caliph, and the emirate became the Caliphate of Córdoba.
